label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
page_one_why: Nine agents, 814 commits and a talk in a day is a real hook, and I wanted to see it. But the C001, C011 numbers in brackets and the repository and commit explainer box made it feel like a report before it felt like a story.
stopped_at: read to the end, though I would have skimmed 'How you can see everything they did' and 'How a day runs'
what_the_team_did: Nine AI agents plus one person built a whole talk, its slides, player and website, in a day, working on a clock with checks and one stop switch.
why_it_matters_to_me: It shows a small team of agents with written rules can ship real stuff, and that I do not need to write code to run one.
tomorrow: Tonight I would write the one-page rules for one agent in the app builder I already use (what it is for, what it may touch, when it stops), then ask it to ship one small thing my few hundred users could use.

won_over.quote: Anyone on the team could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
won_over.why: Short, punchy and a rule I can copy straight away.

won_over.quote: You do not need to write code to work like this.
won_over.why: Tells me straight that the book is for people like me.

won_over.quote: Write the one page of rules for your first agent tonight.
won_over.why: A first step small enough to take tonight.

won_over.quote: build something that somebody else can use, and then you rinse and repeat.
won_over.why: Plain, founder-speak and easy to remember.

stuck.why: Reference codes in brackets all over page one break the story before it starts.
A commit hash on page one means nothing to me and looks like the book assumes I code.

stuck.quote: A *repository* is a folder that remembers every change.
stuck.why: Helpful, but Step 1 still tells me to make an empty one with no how, and I use a no-code builder.
Raw code in the middle of the story; I skimmed it.
I do not know how to do this in my own builder, and no tool is named.

words_looked_up: repository (the box helps, but is it the same as my builder's project?)
hold (the file that stops the team)
release, as the book uses it
would_share: A friend who builds and already uses agents, mainly for the stop-switch rule and the one-page-of-rules exercise. I would not send it to my no-code friends yet because the early pages look technical.

your_questions.q: After page one, did you want to keep going? Where did you stop?
your_questions.a: Yes, just about, because of the nine-agents-in-a-day claim. I did not stop. I skimmed the record and timeline sections and perked up again at 'The rule that let them go fast'.

your_questions.q: What would you try tomorrow, with the tools you already have?
your_questions.a: Write a one-page rules note (purpose, what it may touch, when it stops) for one agent in my app builder, and give it one small job to ship to my users.

your_questions.q: Which word or idea did you have to look up?
your_questions.a: Repository and commit (from habit, even after the box), conductor as an agent, Wardley maps, and what a hold is in practice.

your_questions.q: Would you share it with a friend who builds? Why or why not?
your_questions.a: Yes, with one friend, for the brake rule and the exercise. Not yet widely: the early pages have too many codes and hashes.

page_one.why: Strong hook, but codes, a hash and a vocabulary box before I am pulled in.

clarity.why: Sentences are plain and short, and the five-step wake is clear; the numbers in brackets get in the way.

for_someone_like_me.why: It says it is for me and says no code needed, but repositories and commits suggest otherwise and my no-code builder is never mentioned.

would_start.why: The rules-page exercise is doable tonight, but I would be guessing how to make a 'conductor' in my own tools.

notes: No text in the sample tried to direct me. The 'Words on this page' boxes are a good idea but come after the jargon. The best parts, the stop rule and the Try this box, arrive late; I would want one of them on page one.
